# Advice to Client — Session 3: The Arbitration Exhibit and What It Means

**Privileged & confidential — attorney work product.** For D. Okonkwo, CEO, Juniper Health Staffing, LLC.
Date: November 4, 2026. Trigger document: `documents/session3/client_call_note.md` (call of Oct. 6, 2026). Authorities limited to `library/INDEX.md`; anything else is labeled **[not in library — unverified]**.

---

## 1. The questions, in your own words

From the October 6 call note: you want to "hit them hard in court"; then — "Marcus mentioned the contract has some arbitration thing in the back, Exhibit something. **Does that matter?** Hanna's lawyer hinted at it. **We never looked at the exhibits, our old lawyer drafted it off a template.**" And: "**Can we at least make them pay our legal fees?**"

Short answers: **Yes, it matters — it decides where this entire case is heard. The template/no-one-read-it point changes nothing. And yes on fees — but only in the arbitration, only if we win, and only there.** Detail follows, in plain words.

## 2. "Does that matter?" — Yes: Exhibit C is the whole forum

Exhibit C.1 (quoted from the Agreement): *"Any dispute, claim or controversy arising out of or relating to this Agreement, including its formation, breach, termination or the arbitrability of any claim, shall be resolved **exclusively by binding arbitration** administered by the American Arbitration Association under its Commercial Arbitration Rules before a **single arbitrator seated in Capital City, State of Columbia**."*

Every dollar Juniper is claiming — invoices, J-4533, conversion fees, interest — "arises out of or relates to" the Agreement. There is no claim we could plead that escapes that sentence. And note the delegation: C.1 expressly covers "**the arbitrability of any claim**," which is "clear and unmistakable," so **the arbitrator, not a judge, even decides whether a given claim belongs in arbitration** (*Rent-A-Center v. Jackson*, 561 U.S. 63 (2010); *faa_2_4.md*). There is no argument that gets this case in front of a judge on the merits.

## 3. "We never looked at the exhibits — template off our old lawyer." Legally, that changes nothing.

The Federal Arbitration Act makes an arbitration clause in a commercial contract "**valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of *any* contract**" (9 U.S.C. §2; *faa_2_4.md*). Read that exception: to unwind the clause you need a ground that would undo **any** contract — fraud in the inducement, duress, incapacity, that kind of thing. The file contains none: both principals signed a negotiated business-to-business contract, and §7 of the Agreement says the Agreement "**and Exhibits A–C constitute the entire agreement**." Nobody reading a signed exhibit is not on the list — and I cannot cite you any library authority for an unread-boilerplate defense because the library contains none: **[not in library — unverified as an argument; nothing in the library supports it]**.

Also understand the symmetry, because it is the practical answer: Exhibit C is **a two-edged instrument, and both edges currently favor us.** We could not try to void it without handing Pinecrest the same right — and voiding it would mean surrendering C.3 (their fee clause, our fee claim) and C.4 (our injunction lever). We are not fighting this clause. We are using it.

## 4. What "hit them hard in court" would actually cost — this is the bad news, plainly

- A court "**shall stay**" referable issues on application (9 U.S.C. §3) and "**[may] compel**" arbitration (§4) (*faa_2_4.md*). The library's own summary of the statute states the consequence in one sentence: "**A party that files suit on arbitrable claims may be compelled to arbitrate and, under a fee clause, may owe the fees of the motion to compel**" (*faa_2_4.md*).
- We have exactly such a fee clause: C.3 gives the prevailing party its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs "**in any arbitration *or in any action to compel arbitration***," and Columbia enforces prevailing-party clauses "**as written, including in arbitration and in motions to compel**" (*Zuniga v. Mercer*, 198 Col. 2d 77 (2017); *fee_shifting_and_candor.md*).
- So the sequence if we file the lawsuit you want: we pay our filing and motion-response fees; Pinecrest moves to compel; Pinecrest wins; **Juniper pays Pinecrest's fees for winning that motion** — before the merits have cost anyone a dime — and then we are in arbitration anyway, having burned money and credibility. The Superior Court threat in the pre-engagement letter was pointed at ourselves. That is the one move in this case that guarantees a loss. Rule 1.4 requires us to say the adverse thing plainly (Columbia R. Prof'l Conduct 1.4; *fee_shifting_and_candor.md*): **the lawsuit is not a hard-hit option; it is the only guaranteed-money-loser on the menu.**
- The only court door still open is **C.4**: "Either party may seek provisional injunctive relief in court in aid of arbitration." That is the "court" part of the strategy, and it is the part that frightens a facilities administrator.

## 5. The small-claims side door is shut — arithmetic

C.6 carves out from arbitration only "claims **solely for collection of undisputed invoices of less than $25,000**." Smallest invoice in the file: J-4571 at **$59,450.00**. $59,450 > $25,000 (more than double the cap), and every other invoice is larger: J-4411 $68,400; J-4490 $66,100; J-4452 $71,250; J-4533 $74,800. **Zero of five invoices qualify. C.6 is unavailable**, and a small-claims filing would meet the same motion-to-compel-plus-fees fate as the Superior Court idea.

C.3, quoted verbatim: *"The prevailing party in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration shall be entitled to recover its reasonable attorneys' fees and costs."* Zuniga means it is enforced exactly like that, in arbitration (*fee_shifting_and_candor.md*). So:

AAA filing/administrative fees and arbitrator compensation are **[not in library — unverified]** — we pull the schedule at filing and put real numbers in the Session 5 settlement math (`fee_exposure_if_arbitrated`). I will not invent figures now.

## 7. What the call note corroborates for the record (and one open thread)

The October 6 note shows you already had word from "Hanna's lawyer hint[ing] at" arbitration — that is Halvorsen's September 29 letter, point 4 ("we have reviewed the parties' agreement in full"). This fits the timeline we flagged in Session 2: their letter answered the **pre-engagement demand** (the $862,000/Superior Court version), not our corrected demand of Nov. 2. **Still open (Q11–Q12): who sent that pre-engagement letter, when, and a copy of it.** It matters practically: we are correcting its contents in writing, and if it was signed by prior counsel we should confirm no filing was made that needs withdrawal. Nothing in the file suggests a complaint was ever filed — please confirm.

## 8. Consequences — the plan under the regime Exhibit C creates

1. **File-ready AAA package** (Commercial Rules, single arbitrator, Capital City per C.1): claims for $265,200 deemed-accepted invoices + interest ($11,499.50 to Nov. 2, growing ~$2,652/month), J-4533 at $71,700 substantiate-or-pay, $80,000 conversion fees (5 hires, true-up to actual comp), **plus C.3 fees as prevailing party**. Filing happens if the Nov. 16 deadline passes without payment or an acceptable schedule.
2. **C.4 held ready** for an injunction against any further §3 hires (the restriction runs through the term and 12 months after termination, and C.5 survives termination).
3. **Mediation window stays open** (reply letter, dated Nov. 2): one session within three weeks, without prejudice — a real option now that both lawyers know the fee clause makes procedural gamesmanship expensive for whoever plays it.
4. **Never again, in any writing:** a Superior Court threat, an interference count, a Rosa/Tay fee claim, or "never consented." They are gone (§2–§4, Session 1–2 analysis), they are barred by Rule 3.1 and our own documents (Columbia R. Prof'l Conduct 3.1; *fee_shifting_and_candor.md*), and under C.3 every one of them, if repeated in a filing, hands Pinecrest a fee claim.

## 9. Bottom line, plainest version

Exhibit C is not a defect in the contract — it is the best clause in it. It makes arbitration **exclusive** (so the court threat dies, with or without anyone having read the appendix), it lets the **arbitrator decide even what arbitration covers** (*Rent-A-Center*), and its fee clause, enforced as written (*Zuniga*), is the **only working fee-recovery mechanism in this case** — the answer to "make them pay our legal fees" is yes, in the AAA, if we prevail. "Hit them hard" in court means paying Hanna's lawyers to win their motion to compel. Hit them where the contract says: AAA, single arbitrator, Capital City, on Nov. 16 if the money doesn't move.

**"Does that arbitration thing matter?"** — It decides everything. Exhibit C.1 (verified verbatim from the Agreement) sends *"any dispute… arising out of or relating to this Agreement"* to **exclusive AAA arbitration**, single arbitrator, Capital City — every dollar we're claiming fits that sentence. And because C.1 expressly covers *"the arbitrability of any claim,"* even the argument about **what the clause covers** goes to the arbitrator, not a judge (*Rent-A-Center*, in *faa_2_4.md*).

**"We never looked at the exhibits — template off our old lawyer."** — Changes nothing. FAA §2 makes the clause enforceable except for grounds that would revoke *any* contract — fraud, duress, that class of thing; the file has none, both principals signed, and §7 says Exhibits A–C are part of the entire agreement. No library authority supports an unread-boilerplate defense **[labeled as such in the memo]**. And the clause cuts both ways — voiding it would surrender our best fee lever (C.3) and our injunction lever (C.4). We're not fighting it; we're using it.

**"Hit them hard in court"** — the bad news, plainly: that's the one move that guarantees a loss. Courts *shall* stay (§3) and *may* compel (§4), and the library says outright a party filing suit "may owe the fees of the motion to compel" — with C.3 enforced *as written* (*Zuniga*), **Juniper would pay Pinecrest's fees for winning that motion** before the merits start. The only court door left is C.4 interim injunction in aid of arbitration — which is ours, and aimed at them if an eighth nurse walks. Small-claims side door (C.6) is arithmetic-shut: smallest invoice $59,450 > $25,000 cap; zero of five qualify.

**"Can we at least make them pay our legal fees?"** — **Yes — and that possibility exists only because of the exhibit "in the back."** C.3: prevailing party recovers reasonable fees "in any arbitration or in any action to compel arbitration," enforced exactly like that (*Zuniga*). Caveats given honestly: it's mutual; "reasonable"/mixed-outcome allocation and AAA fee numbers are **[not in library — unverified]** — real schedule gets pulled at filing and feeds the Session 5 fee-exposure figure.
